<!--
  Unit 09 · Happy Randomization

  Three simulations that show why random assignment does not guarantee balanced groups,
  and why a balance table with many rows needs an adjusted decision rule.

  Every number and figure on the page is computed by the R code in this file, with fixed
  seeds, so the page re-renders identically. The page body is written as raw HTML blocks
  (```{=html}) so it shares the styling of the course notes pages; figures, tables, and
  code sit between those blocks as ordinary R chunks.

  Render with:  rmarkdown::render("happy-randomization.rmd")
-->

```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  echo = FALSE, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE,
  dev = "png", dpi = 200, fig.retina = 1,
  fig.width = 6.5, fig.height = 3.2
)

# ---- palette and plot scaffolding --------------------------------------------

blue   <- "#3f77b1"
orange <- "#dd7a35"
slate  <- "#5e6878"
red    <- "#b23a48"
light  <- "#b1b8bf"
gridc  <- "#ececec"

fig_par <- function() {
  par(mar = c(3.1, 3.6, 0.6, 0.8), mgp = c(2.1, 0.55, 0), las = 1,
      tcl = -0.3, cex.axis = 0.8, cex.lab = 0.85, bty = "l")
}

# Empty plot with light gridlines, left/bottom axes only.
# Pass xat + xlabels for a categorical x-axis.
fig_frame <- function(xlim, ylim, xlab, ylab, yat = pretty(ylim),
                      xat = NULL, xlabels = NULL) {
  fig_par()
  plot(NA, xlim = xlim, ylim = ylim, xlab = xlab, ylab = ylab,
       axes = FALSE, xaxs = "i", yaxs = "i")
  abline(h = yat, col = gridc, lwd = 0.8)
  if (is.null(xlabels)) {
    xt <- pretty(xlim)
    abline(v = xt, col = gridc, lwd = 0.8)
    axis(1, at = xt, lwd = 0, lwd.ticks = 1)
  } else {
    abline(v = xat, col = gridc, lwd = 0.8)
    axis(1, at = xat, labels = xlabels, lwd = 0, lwd.ticks = 1)
  }
  axis(2, at = yat, lwd = 0, lwd.ticks = 1)
  box(bty = "l")
}

dot <- function(x, y, col, cex = 1.5) {
  points(x, y, pch = 21, bg = col, col = "white", cex = cex, lwd = 1.2)
}

legend_tl <- function(labels, cols, lty = 1, lwd = 3, pch = NA, pt.bg = NA,
                      where = "topleft") {
  legend(where, legend = labels, col = cols, lty = lty, lwd = lwd,
         pch = pch, pt.bg = pt.bg, bty = "n", cex = 0.75, seg.len = 1.6,
         inset = c(0.01, 0.02))
}

# ---- formatting helpers for inline numbers and HTML tables ---------------------

pct  <- function(x, d = 0) paste0(formatC(100 * x, format = "f", digits = d), "%")
num  <- function(x, d = 1) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = d, big.mark = ",")
pval <- function(p) ifelse(p < 0.001, "&lt; 0.001", formatC(p, format = "f", digits = 3))

# Emit a raw HTML block from inside an R chunk (use with results = "asis").
html <- function(...) cat("\n```{=html}\n", ..., "\n```\n", sep = "")

```{r sim-functions, include=FALSE}
# ---- shared simulation functions (shown again in the code boxes below) ---------

# Random assignment: shuffle equal numbers of each group label across the blocks.
assign_groups <- function(n.blocks, n.groups = 5) {
  sample(rep(paste("Group", 1:n.groups), length.out = n.blocks))
}

# Every pairwise t-test between groups: n(n - 1) / 2 contrasts.
pairwise_tests <- function(y, group) {
  pairs <- combn(sort(unique(group)), 2)
  data.frame(
    g1      = pairs[1, ],
    g2      = pairs[2, ],
    diff    = apply(pairs, 2, function(p) mean(y[group == p[1]]) - mean(y[group == p[2]])),
    p.value = apply(pairs, 2, function(p) t.test(y[group == p[1]], y[group == p[2]])$p.value)
  )
}
```

```{r part1, include=FALSE}
# ---- Part 1: five groups of ten blocks -----------------------------------------

set.seed(2026)
blocks <- data.frame(block = 1:50, score = round(rnorm(50, mean = 50, sd = 10)))

# One randomization to look at closely. We search for the first seed whose draw
# contains exactly one significant contrast, so the example shows a false alarm.
seed <- 1
repeat {
  set.seed(seed)
  blocks$group <- assign_groups(50)
  tests <- pairwise_tests(blocks$score, blocks$group)
  if (sum(tests$p.value < 0.05) == 1) break
  seed <- seed + 1
}
group.means <- tapply(blocks$score, blocks$group, mean)
sig.row     <- tests[tests$p.value < 0.05, ]

# The same randomization repeated 5,000 times.
set.seed(1)
n.sig <- replicate(5000, {
  group <- assign_groups(50)
  sum(pairwise_tests(blocks$score, group)$p.value < 0.05)
})
# Keep the full results of the first 100 lotteries to draw as a grid.
set.seed(100)
grid.tests <- replicate(100, simplify = FALSE,
                        pairwise_tests(blocks$score, assign_groups(50)))
grid.any   <- sapply(grid.tests, function(t) any(t$p.value < 0.05))

avg.sig  <- mean(n.sig)
any.sig  <- mean(n.sig > 0)
dist.sig <- table(factor(pmin(n.sig, 3), levels = 0:3)) / length(n.sig)
```

```{r part1b, include=FALSE}
# ---- Part 1b: the same design with larger groups -------------------------------

sizes <- c(10, 25, 50, 100, 250, 1000)          # blocks per group

converge <- lapply(sizes, function(n) {
  set.seed(n)
  score <- rnorm(5 * n, mean = 50, sd = 10)      # a population of 5n blocks
  sims <- replicate(1000, {
    group <- assign_groups(5 * n)
    means <- tapply(score, group, mean) - mean(score)
    c(gap = max(means) - min(means),
      any.sig = any(pairwise_tests(score, group)$p.value < 0.05),
      means)
  })
  list(n = n, gap = mean(sims["gap", ]), any.sig = mean(sims["any.sig", ]),
       se = sd(score) / sqrt(n),
       deviations = as.vector(sims[-(1:2), 1:200]))  # group means from 200 draws
})
conv <- do.call(rbind, lapply(converge, function(x)
  data.frame(n = x$n, gap = x$gap, se = x$se, any.sig = x$any.sig)))
```

```{r part2, include=FALSE}
# ---- Part 2: treatment vs control, 1 to 20 covariates --------------------------

# One simulated study population: n students and 20 baseline attributes.
make_students <- function(n) {
  data.frame(
    mother.educ     = rnorm(n, 13, 2.5),          # years of schooling
    father.educ     = rnorm(n, 13, 2.8),
    family.income   = rlnorm(n, log(55), 0.6),    # $1,000s
    black           = rbinom(n, 1, 0.15),
    hispanic        = rbinom(n, 1, 0.25),
    asian           = rbinom(n, 1, 0.06),
    female          = rbinom(n, 1, 0.50),
    free.lunch      = rbinom(n, 1, 0.45),
    english.learner = rbinom(n, 1, 0.10),
    special.ed      = rbinom(n, 1, 0.13),
    prior.math      = rnorm(n, 50, 10),
    prior.reading   = rnorm(n, 50, 10),
    age.months      = rnorm(n, 120, 4),
    days.absent     = rpois(n, 8),
    household.size  = 2 + rpois(n, 2),
    single.parent   = rbinom(n, 1, 0.30),
    changed.school  = rbinom(n, 1, 0.12),
    books.at.home   = rpois(n, 40),
    homework.hours  = rgamma(n, 2, 0.4),
    preschool       = rbinom(n, 1, 0.60)
  )
}

set.seed(2026)
studies <- replicate(1000, simplify = FALSE, {
  students <- make_students(200)
  treat    <- sample(rep(0:1, each = 100))       # 100 treated, 100 controls

  # one t-test per covariate
  p <- sapply(students, function(x) t.test(x[treat == 1], x[treat == 0])$p.value)

  # omnibus alternative: regress treatment on the first k covariates, joint F-test
  f.p <- sapply(1:20, function(k) {
    f <- summary(lm(treat ~ ., data = students[1:k]))$fstatistic
    pf(f[1], f[2], f[3], lower.tail = FALSE)
  })
  list(p = p, f.p = f.p)
})

P  <- t(sapply(studies, `[[`, "p"))    # 1,000 studies x 20 covariates
FP <- t(sapply(studies, `[[`, "f.p"))  # 1,000 studies x 20 joint tests

k <- 1:20
n.sig.k  <- lapply(k, function(j) rowSums(P[, 1:j, drop = FALSE] < 0.05))
n.bonf.k <- lapply(k, function(j) rowSums(P[, 1:j, drop = FALSE] < 0.05 / j))

results <- data.frame(
  k        = k,
  any.sig  = sapply(n.sig.k, function(x) mean(x > 0)),
  avg.sig  = sapply(n.sig.k, mean),
  expected = 1 - 0.95^k,
  bonf     = sapply(n.bonf.k, function(x) mean(x > 0)),
  joint.F  = colMeans(FP < 0.05)
)
```

```{r demo-table, include=FALSE}
# ---- One study for the demo balance table (5 covariates) -----------------------

# Search for the first seed whose table has exactly one row significant at .05
# that does not survive the Bonferroni threshold of .05 / 5 = .01.
demo.vars <- c("mother.educ", "family.income", "black", "free.lunch", "prior.math")
seed <- 1
repeat {
  set.seed(seed)
  students <- make_students(200)[demo.vars]
  treat    <- sample(rep(0:1, each = 100))
  demo <- data.frame(
    treat.mean = sapply(students, function(x) mean(x[treat == 1])),
    ctrl.mean  = sapply(students, function(x) mean(x[treat == 0])),
    p.value    = sapply(students, function(x) t.test(x[treat == 1], x[treat == 0])$p.value)
  )
  if (sum(demo$p.value < 0.05) == 1 && all(demo$p.value >= 0.01)) break
  seed <- seed + 1
}

# Joint F-test: do the five covariates together predict treatment assignment?
demo.f   <- summary(lm(treat ~ ., data = students))$fstatistic
demo.f.p <- pf(demo.f[1], demo.f[2], demo.f[3], lower.tail = FALSE)
```

```{r figures, include=FALSE}
# ---- figure functions ----------------------------------------------------------

fig_one_draw <- function() {
  set.seed(11)
  gx <- as.integer(sub("Group ", "", blocks$group))
  fig_frame(c(0.4, 5.6), c(20, 80), "", "Block average prior score",
            yat = seq(20, 80, 10), xat = 1:5, xlabels = names(group.means))
  abline(h = mean(blocks$score), col = slate, lty = 2, lwd = 1.5)
  points(gx + runif(50, -0.18, 0.18), blocks$score, pch = 16,
         col = adjustcolor(blue, 0.5), cex = 0.95)
  segments(1:5 - 0.3, group.means, 1:5 + 0.3, group.means, col = orange, lwd = 3)
  text(1:5, 76, paste("mean", num(group.means)), cex = 0.75, col = orange, font = 2)
}

# ---- contrast diagrams: 5 groups as a pentagon, 10 contrasts as its sides and star ----

gray.edge <- "#9aa1a9"
node.fill <- "#d4d7db"

# Node positions: Group 1 at the top, then clockwise.
k5_xy <- function(cx = 0, cy = 0, r = 1) {
  a <- (90 - 72 * (0:4)) * pi / 180
  cbind(x = cx + r * cos(a), y = cy + r * sin(a))
}

# Draw the 10 contrasts of one lottery: gray if p >= .05, red if p < .05.
draw_k5 <- function(tests, cx = 0, cy = 0, r = 1, lwd = c(1.6, 4), node.cex = 4.2,
                    node.labels = TRUE) {
  xy  <- k5_xy(cx, cy, r)
  i1  <- as.integer(sub("Group ", "", tests$g1))
  i2  <- as.integer(sub("Group ", "", tests$g2))
  sig <- tests$p.value < 0.05
  ord <- order(sig)                                # draw red lines on top
  segments(xy[i1[ord], 1], xy[i1[ord], 2], xy[i2[ord], 1], xy[i2[ord], 2],
           col = ifelse(sig[ord], red, gray.edge), lwd = ifelse(sig[ord], lwd[2], lwd[1]))
  points(xy, pch = 21, bg = node.fill, col = "#4d565f", cex = node.cex, lwd = 1.2)
  if (node.labels) text(xy, labels = 1:5, cex = 0.95, font = 2, col = "#1f2429")
  invisible(xy)
}

fig_k5_big <- function() {
  par(mar = c(0, 0, 0, 0))
  plot(NA, xlim = c(-3, 3), ylim = c(-1.62, 1.66), asp = 1, axes = FALSE, xlab = "", ylab = "")
  xy <- draw_k5(tests)

  # group means just outside each node
  lab.xy <- k5_xy(r = 1.34)
  text(lab.xy, labels = num(group.means), cex = 0.8, font = 2, col = orange)

  note <- function(x, y, label, adj) text(x, y, label, adj = adj, cex = 0.72, col = slate)
  pointer <- function(x0, y0, x1, y1) arrows(x0, y0, x1, y1, length = 0.06, col = slate, lwd = 1)

  # the significant contrast (left, top)
  s  <- tests[tests$p.value < 0.05, ][1, ]
  i1 <- as.integer(sub("Group ", "", s$g1)); i2 <- as.integer(sub("Group ", "", s$g2))
  mid <- colMeans(xy[c(i1, i2), ])
  text(-2.95, 1.42, "Red line = significant contrast", adj = c(0, 0.5), cex = 0.74,
       col = red, font = 2)
  note(-2.95, 1.2, paste0(s$g1, " vs ", s$g2, ": gap of ", num(abs(s$diff)),
                          " points,\np = ", pval(s$p.value)), adj = c(0, 1))
  pointer(-1.75, 1.05, mid[1] - 0.04, mid[2] + 0.04)

  # a non-significant contrast (left, bottom): the bottom side, 3 vs 4
  text(-2.95, -1.12, "Gray line = contrast not\nsignificant (p ≥ .05)", adj = c(0, 1),
       cex = 0.74, col = "#4d565f", font = 2)
  pointer(-1.6, -1.2, -0.15, -0.83)

  # a node (right, top)
  text(2.95, 1.42, "Circle = one study group", adj = c(1, 0.5), cex = 0.74,
       col = "#1f2429", font = 2)
  note(2.95, 1.2, "10 classroom blocks,\nrandomly assigned", adj = c(1, 1))
  pointer(1.6, 1.3, 0.2, 1.02)

  # a mean label (right, middle)
  text(2.95, -0.2, "Orange number = the group's\nmean prior score", adj = c(1, 1),
       cex = 0.74, col = orange, font = 2)
  pointer(1.75, -0.12, 1.42, 0.3)

  # the count (right, bottom)
  note(2.95, -1.12, "Every line is one t-test.\n5 groups × 4 / 2 = 10 lines", adj = c(1, 1))
}

fig_k5_grid <- function() {
  par(mar = c(0, 0, 0, 0))
  plot(NA, xlim = c(0.45, 10.55), ylim = c(-10.55, -0.45), asp = 1, axes = FALSE,
       xlab = "", ylab = "")
  for (j in seq_along(grid.tests)) {
    col <- (j - 1) %% 10 + 1; row <- (j - 1) %/% 10 + 1
    if (grid.any[j]) rect(col - 0.47, -row - 0.47, col + 0.47, -row + 0.47,
                          col = adjustcolor(red, 0.08), border = adjustcolor(red, 0.45), lwd = 0.8)
    draw_k5(grid.tests[[j]], cx = col, cy = -row + 0.02, r = 0.34, lwd = c(0.7, 1.9),
            node.cex = 0.6, node.labels = FALSE)
  }
}

fig_converge <- function() {
  fig_frame(c(0.4, 6.6), c(-10, 10), "Blocks per group", "Group mean minus overall mean",
            yat = seq(-10, 10, 5), xat = seq_along(sizes), xlabels = sizes)
  abline(h = 0, col = slate, lwd = 1.5)
  set.seed(3)
  for (i in seq_along(converge)) {
    d <- converge[[i]]$deviations
    points(i + runif(length(d), -0.28, 0.28), d, pch = 16,
           col = adjustcolor(blue, 0.18), cex = 0.55)
    segments(i - 0.32, c(-2, 2) * converge[[i]]$se * sqrt(4 / 5),
             i + 0.32, c(-2, 2) * converge[[i]]$se * sqrt(4 / 5), col = orange, lwd = 2.5)
  }
  legend_tl(c("One group's mean, one randomization", "About 95% of group means fall inside"),
            c(adjustcolor(blue, 0.6), orange), lty = c(NA, 1), lwd = c(NA, 2.5),
            pch = c(16, NA), where = "topright")
}

fig_covariates <- function() {
  fig_frame(c(0.5, 20.5), c(0, 70), "Number of covariates in the balance table",
            "Studies flagged as unbalanced (%)", yat = seq(0, 70, 10),
            xat = c(1, 5, 10, 15, 20), xlabels = c(1, 5, 10, 15, 20))
  abline(h = 5, col = red, lty = 3, lwd = 1.5)
  lines(k, 100 * results$expected, col = light, lwd = 2, lty = 2)
  lines(k, 100 * results$any.sig, col = orange, lwd = 3); dot(k, 100 * results$any.sig, orange, cex = 0.9)
  lines(k, 100 * results$bonf, col = blue, lwd = 3);      dot(k, 100 * results$bonf, blue, cex = 0.9)
  lines(k, 100 * results$joint.F, col = slate, lwd = 2)
  legend_tl(c("Any t-test at p < .05", "Theory: 1 - 0.95^k",
              "Any t-test at p < .05 / k (Bonferroni)", "Joint F-test at p < .05",
              "Target: 5%"),
            c(orange, light, blue, slate, red), lty = c(1, 2, 1, 1, 3),
            lwd = c(3, 2, 3, 2, 1.5))
}
```

```{=html}
<div class="wrap">

  <header class="masthead">
    <p class="eyebrow">Research Design</p>
    <h1>Happy Randomization</h1>
    <p class="dek">Random assignment balances groups <em>on average</em>, not in every study. Three
      simulations show how often a perfectly fair lottery produces groups that look different, why
      small groups make it worse, and how to test for balance without fooling yourself when the
      balance table has many rows.</p>
    <nav class="jump" aria-label="Sections">
      <a href="#concepts">Key concepts</a>
      <a href="#group-differences">Group differences</a>
      <a href="#bonferroni">Bonferroni corrections</a>
      <a href="#takeaways">Takeaways</a>
    </nav>
  </header>

  <!-- ================================================================== -->
  <section id="concepts">
    <div class="sec-head">
      <p class="num">Overview</p>
      <h2>Key concepts</h2>
      <p class="sub">Why a study that randomized correctly still has to check its groups.</p>
    </div>

    <div class="concepts">
      <p class="panel-label">The argument in four claims</p>

      <p class="claim">Randomization is fair, not perfect.</p>
      <p>Random assignment guarantees that groups are equal <strong>in expectation</strong>: averaged
        over every possible lottery, no group is favored. Any single lottery can still deal one group
        the stronger students. A study that randomized correctly can be unlucky. When the groups turn
        out comparable we call it <strong>happy randomization</strong>.</p>

      <p class="claim">A 5% test raises a false alarm 5% of the time, by design.</p>
      <p>When the groups really are equivalent in the population, a t-test at
        <span class="m">α = 0.05</span> will still call one contrast in twenty "significant." That is
        what the 0.05 means.</p>

      <p class="claim">More tests, more false alarms.</p>
      <p>Five study groups produce 10 pairwise contrasts, and a balance table with 20 covariates
        produces 20 tests. The chance that <em>at least one</em> of them comes out significant grows
        quickly. When the tests are an omnibus check of equivalence across many covariates, the
        decision rule for the whole table has to be adjusted: divide <span class="m">α</span> by the
        number of tests (Bonferroni), or run one joint test.</p>

      <p class="claim">Big samples shrink imbalances, not false alarms.</p>
      <p>As groups grow, their means converge on each other and the <strong>size</strong> of any chance
        imbalance falls. The <strong>false-alarm rate</strong> of each test stays at 5% at every sample
        size. Small studies are the ones that get substantively unbalanced groups, which is why they
        often stratify the lottery instead of relying on luck.</p>
    </div>

    <h3>Where the question comes from</h3>
    <p>The study described in the Chapter 1 reading randomizes <em>blocks</em> of students (classrooms)
      rather than individual students, and it has only a handful of blocks per study group. Instead of a
      single lottery, it assigns blocks in <strong>tranches</strong>: rank the blocks by prior academic
      performance, take the top tranche and randomly give one block to each study group, then do the
      same with the next tranche, and so on down the list.</p>
    <p>Why go to the trouble? If assignment is random, shouldn't the groups come out balanced anyway?
      The simulations below answer that question.</p>
  </section>

  <!-- ================================================================== -->
  <section id="group-differences">
    <div class="sec-head">
      <p class="num">Section one</p>
      <h2>Group differences after random assignment</h2>
      <p class="sub">Five study groups of ten blocks each: how often a fair lottery produces groups
        that differ, and what changes as the groups grow.</p>
    </div>

    <h3>The setup</h3>
    <p>A district has 50 classroom blocks. For each block we know its average prior-year test score.
      Across all 50 blocks the scores average `r num(mean(blocks$score))` with a standard deviation of
      `r num(sd(blocks$score))`. We randomly assign 10 blocks to each of 5 study groups, and nothing
      about the lottery depends on the scores.</p>

    <figure class="fig">
```

```{r fig-one-draw, fig.alt="Fifty block scores split into five randomly assigned groups of ten, with each group's mean marked."}
fig_one_draw()
```

```{=html}
    </figure>
    <p class="figcap">One random assignment of 50 blocks to 5 groups. Dots are blocks; orange bars are
      group means; the dashed line is the mean of all 50 blocks.</p>
```

```{r tbl-means, results="asis"}
rows <- paste0("<tr><td class=\"l\">", names(group.means), "</td><td>", num(group.means),
               "</td><td>", num(group.means - mean(blocks$score)), "</td></tr>", collapse = "\n")
html('<div class="table-scroll"><table class="num-table">',
     '<caption>Group means after one lottery</caption>',
     '<thead><tr><th>Study group</th><th>Mean prior score</th><th>Gap from overall mean</th></tr></thead>',
     '<tbody>', rows, '</tbody></table></div>')
```

```{=html}
    <p>Same population, same lottery rules, yet the group means span
      `r num(max(group.means) - min(group.means))` points, from `r num(min(group.means))` to
      `r num(max(group.means))`.</p>

    <div class="callout">
      <span class="lbl">Why a group that is too high or too low matters</span>
      <p>Suppose `r names(which.min(group.means))` happened to be the <strong>control group</strong>.
        It starts `r num(mean(blocks$score) - min(group.means))` points below the average block, about
        `r num((mean(blocks$score) - min(group.means)) / sd(blocks$score), 2)` standard deviations. Every
        treatment group would then look better than the control before the program did anything, and the
        study would report that head start as a program effect. If the unlucky draw had put the strongest
        blocks in the control group instead, a real effect could be hidden. In a post-test-only design,
        the comparison groups have to be equivalent at baseline, because the control group is the
        counterfactual.</p>
    </div>

    <p>Is a gap this size unusual, or is it what fair lotteries normally produce? To find out, compare
      every group with every other group.</p>

    <h3>How many contrasts?</h3>
    <p>With <span class="m"><i>g</i></span> groups, the number of distinct pairs is</p>
    <div class="eq center">
      <span class="m">number of contrasts = <i>g</i>(<i>g</i> &minus; 1) / 2</span>
    </div>
    <p>Each group is paired with the <span class="m"><i>g</i> &minus; 1</span> others, and dividing by
      2 removes duplicates (Group 1 vs Group 2 is the same contrast as Group 2 vs Group 1). Five groups
      give <span class="m">5 &times; 4 / 2 = 10</span> contrasts. The count grows much faster than the
      number of groups:</p>
```

```{r tbl-contrasts, results="asis"}
g <- c(2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 10)
cc <- g * (g - 1) / 2
rows <- paste0("<tr", ifelse(g == 5, ' class="flag"', ""), "><td class=\"l\">", g, "</td><td>", cc,
               "</td><td>", num(0.05 * cc, 2), "</td></tr>", collapse = "\n")
html('<div class="table-scroll"><table class="num-table">',
     '<caption>Contrasts grow with the square of the number of groups</caption>',
     '<thead><tr><th>Groups</th><th>Pairwise contrasts</th>',
     '<th>Contrasts expected to be significant by chance at <span class="m">α = .05</span></th></tr></thead>',
     '<tbody>', rows, '</tbody></table></div>')
```

```{=html}
    <h3>Testing all ten contrasts</h3>
    <p>The 10 contrasts are easiest to see as a picture. Put the five groups at the corners of a
      pentagon and draw a line between every pair: the five sides plus the five-pointed star inside
      (a pentagram) are exactly the 10 contrasts. Each line is one t-test of the difference in mean
      prior scores between the two groups it connects.</p>

    <figure class="fig wide">
```

```{r fig-k5-big, fig.width=7.5, fig.height=4.1, fig.alt="Five numbered circles at the corners of a pentagon, joined by ten lines. Nine lines are gray; the line between Group 1 and Group 5 is red, marking the one significant contrast."}
fig_k5_big()
```

```{=html}
    </figure>
    <p class="figcap">The lottery shown above, drawn as a contrast diagram. Each of the 10 lines is a
      two-sample t-test between the groups at its ends.</p>
```

```{r tbl-pairs, results="asis"}
flag <- tests$p.value < 0.05
rows <- paste0("<tr", ifelse(flag, ' class="flag"', ""), "><td class=\"l\">", tests$g1, " vs ",
               tests$g2, "</td><td>", num(tests$diff), "</td><td", ifelse(flag, ' class="hi"', ""),
               ">", pval(tests$p.value), "</td></tr>", collapse = "\n")
html('<div class="table-scroll"><table class="num-table">',
     '<caption>The same 10 contrasts as a table</caption>',
     '<thead><tr><th>Contrast</th><th>Difference in means</th><th>p-value</th></tr></thead>',
     '<tbody>', rows, '</tbody></table></div>')
```

```{=html}
    <p>One contrast, `r sig.row$g1` vs `r sig.row$g2`, is significant at the 5% level
      (p = `r pval(sig.row$p.value)`). `r names(which.min(group.means))` drew mostly low-scoring blocks
      and `r names(which.max(group.means))` drew mostly high-scoring ones. Nothing went wrong: every
      group came from the same 50 blocks through a fair process. That is simply what happens in some
      lotteries. (We chose this lottery because it contains a significant contrast, so the example has
      something to show. The next step reports how often that happens.)</p>

    <h3>Repeat the lottery 5,000 times</h3>
    <p>To see what is typical, we rerun the random assignment 5,000 times on the same 50 blocks and
      count how many of the 10 contrasts come out significant each time.</p>

    <div class="stats">
      <div class="stat"><span class="big">`r num(avg.sig, 2)`</span>
        <span class="what">significant contrasts per lottery, on average (expected:
          10 &times; 0.05 = 0.50)</span></div>
      <div class="stat"><span class="big">`r pct(any.sig)`</span>
        <span class="what">of lotteries show at least one significant contrast</span></div>
      <div class="stat"><span class="big">`r pct(dist.sig[["0"]])`</span>
        <span class="what">of lotteries pass all 10 tests</span></div>
    </div>

    <p>Here are the first 100 of those lotteries, each drawn as its own contrast diagram. In
      `r sum(grid.any)` of the 100, at least one line is red (shaded panels).</p>

    <figure class="fig wide">
```

```{r fig-k5-grid, fig.width=7, fig.height=7, fig.alt="A ten by ten grid of small pentagon contrast diagrams. Most have only gray lines; roughly a quarter are shaded and contain one or more red lines."}
fig_k5_grid()
```

```{=html}
    </figure>
    <p class="figcap">100 random assignments of the same 50 blocks. Red lines are contrasts significant
      at p &lt; .05; shaded panels contain at least one. Every one of these lotteries was fair.</p>
```

```{r tbl-dist, results="asis"}
labs <- c("0", "1", "2", "3 or more")
rows <- paste0("<tr><td class=\"l\">", labs, "</td><td>", pct(as.numeric(dist.sig), 1),
               "</td></tr>", collapse = "\n")
html('<div class="table-scroll"><table class="num-table">',
     '<caption>Significant contrasts per lottery, 5,000 lotteries</caption>',
     '<thead><tr><th>Number significant (of 10)</th><th>Share of lotteries</th></tr></thead>',
     '<tbody>', rows, '</tbody></table></div>')
```

```{=html}
    <p>The average of `r num(avg.sig, 2)` is what the arithmetic predicts: 10 tests, each with
      a 5% chance of a false alarm, gives 0.5 expected false alarms. Put another way, <strong>roughly
      `r pct(any.sig)` of perfectly valid randomizations would "fail" a balance check that uses
      p &lt; .05 for each contrast.</strong></p>

    <div class="callout">
      <span class="lbl">Why `r pct(any.sig)` and not 40%?</span>
      <p>If the 10 tests were independent, the chance of at least one false alarm would be
        <span class="m">1 &minus; 0.95<sup>10</sup> = 40%</span>. They are not independent: every group
        appears in four contrasts, so one unusual group tends to set off several tests at once (note the
        lotteries with 2 or more). Overlapping tests produce fewer lotteries with
        <em>any</em> alarm, but the <em>average</em> number of alarms is still 0.5.</p>
    </div>
```

    <details class="code">
      <summary>R code: one lottery and 5,000 repeats</summary>
```

```

```{=html}
    </details>

    <h3 id="bigger">What changes when the groups get bigger</h3>
    <p>Now keep the design (5 groups, random assignment) but vary the number of blocks per group from 10
      to 1,000. For each size we draw a population of blocks with mean 50 and standard deviation 10, run
      the lottery 1,000 times, and record two things: how far apart the group means land, and whether
      any of the 10 contrasts is significant.</p>

    <figure class="fig">
```

```{r fig-converge, fig.alt="Group means scattered around the overall mean, with the scatter shrinking sharply as blocks per group rise from 10 to 1000."}
fig_converge()
```

```{=html}
    </figure>
    <p class="figcap">Each dot is one group's mean (minus the overall mean) from one of 200 lotteries.
      The spread shrinks in proportion to <span class="m">1 / &radic;<i>n</i></span>.</p>
```

```{r tbl-converge, results="asis"}
rows <- paste0("<tr><td class=\"l\">", conv$n, "</td><td>", num(conv$se, 2), "</td><td class=\"ok\">",
               num(conv$gap, 2), "</td><td>", pct(conv$any.sig), "</td></tr>", collapse = "\n")
html('<div class="table-scroll"><table class="num-table">',
     '<caption>Five groups, 1,000 lotteries at each size</caption>',
     '<thead><tr><th>Blocks per group</th><th>Standard error of a group mean</th>',
     '<th>Average gap, highest minus lowest group mean</th>',
     '<th>Lotteries with at least one significant contrast</th></tr></thead>',
     '<tbody>', rows, '</tbody></table></div>')
```

```{=html}
    <p>Read the two right-hand columns together:</p>
    <ul>
      <li><strong>The gap shrinks.</strong> With 10 blocks per group, the best and worst groups differ
        by about `r num(conv$gap[1], 1)` points on average, which is
        `r num(conv$gap[1] / 10, 2)` standard deviations, large enough to swamp a modest program effect.
        With 1,000 blocks per group the gap is `r num(conv$gap[6], 2)` points. This is the law of large
        numbers at work: every group mean converges on the population mean, so they converge on each
        other.</li>
      <li><strong>The false-alarm rate does not.</strong> About `r pct(mean(conv$any.sig))` of lotteries
        show a significant contrast at every size. The t-test measures differences relative to their
        standard error, and the standard error shrinks just as fast as the gap does.</li>
    </ul>

    <div class="callout">
      <span class="lbl">The lesson for small studies</span>
      <p>Large samples do not make the balance test easier to pass. They make the imbalances you
        <em>do</em> get too small to matter. In a study with only 10 blocks per group, a chance gap of
        several points is common, and the outcome comparison inherits it. That is why the study in the
        reading assigned blocks in tranches: <strong>stratified (blocked) randomization</strong> forces
        each group to get one block from each performance level, so balance on prior scores is
        guaranteed by construction rather than left to luck.</p>
    </div>

    <details class="code">
      <summary>R code: larger groups</summary>

```{=html}
    </details>
  </section>

  <!-- ================================================================== -->
  <section id="bonferroni">
    <div class="sec-head">
      <p class="num">Section two</p>
      <h2>Bonferroni corrections for balance tables</h2>
      <p class="sub">Two groups, many covariates. A balance table is a set of tests run together, and
        its decision rule has to account for how many there are.</p>
    </div>

    <h3>A typical balance table</h3>
    <p>A study of a tutoring program randomly assigns 200 students: 100 to treatment and 100 to
      control. Before the program starts, it measures baseline attributes that could affect test
      scores, to check balance and to use as controls later. Published studies report this check as a
      balance table: one row per attribute, the mean in each group, the difference, and a test of that
      difference. Here is one for five of the attributes.</p>
```

```{r tbl-demo, results="asis"}
demo.lab <- c("Mother's education (years)", "Family income ($1,000s)", "Black = 1",
              "Free or reduced-price lunch = 1", "Prior math score")
demo.dig <- c(1, 1, 2, 2, 1)
demo.short <- c("mother's education", "family income", "the share of Black students",
                "free or reduced-price lunch eligibility", "prior math scores")
star <- ifelse(demo$p.value < 0.05, "*", "")
rows <- paste0("<tr", ifelse(star == "*", ' class="flag"', ""), "><td class=\"l\">", demo.lab,
               "</td><td>", mapply(num, demo$treat.mean, demo.dig), "</td><td>",
               mapply(num, demo$ctrl.mean, demo.dig), "</td><td>",
               mapply(num, demo$treat.mean - demo$ctrl.mean, demo.dig), "</td><td",
               ifelse(star == "*", ' class="hi"', ""), ">", formatC(demo$p.value, format = "f", digits = 3),
               star, "</td></tr>", collapse = "\n")
html('<div class="table-scroll"><table class="num-table pub">',
     '<caption>Table 1. Balance between treatment and control students at baseline</caption>',
     '<thead><tr><th>Student characteristic</th><th>Treatment<br>(N = 100)</th>',
     '<th>Control<br>(N = 100)</th><th>Difference</th><th>p-value</th></tr></thead>',
     '<tbody>', rows, '</tbody>',
     '<tfoot><tr><td class="l" colspan="4">Joint F-test of all five characteristics, F(',
     demo.f[2], ', ', demo.f[3], ') = ', num(demo.f[1], 2), '</td><td>',
     formatC(demo.f.p, format = "f", digits = 3), '</td></tr></tfoot></table>',
     '<p class="tnote"><em>Source:</em> simulated data.<br>* Significant at the 5 percent level.<br>',
     'The joint F-test regresses the treatment indicator on all five characteristics and tests whether ',
     'they jointly predict assignment.</p></div>')
```

```{=html}
    <p>Read the way most balance tables are read, the star says the groups differ on
      `r demo.short[demo$p.value < 0.05]`, so the randomization looks unhappy. But this table
      runs five tests at once. Even if the lottery worked perfectly, the chance that at least one of five
      independent tests comes out significant at the 5% level is</p>
    <div class="eq center">
      <span class="m">1 &minus; (1 &minus; 0.05)<sup>5</sup> = 1 &minus; 0.95<sup>5</sup> = 0.23</span>
    </div>
    <p>So a "starred" row shows up in nearly a quarter of balance tables like this one when nothing is
      wrong. The question a balance table is meant to answer is about the whole table (are the groups
      equivalent?), so the error rate has to be controlled for the whole table, not row by row.</p>

    <h3>The Bonferroni correction</h3>
    <p>The Bonferroni correction keeps the overall false-alarm rate at
      <span class="m">α</span> by dividing it among the <span class="m"><i>k</i></span> tests:</p>
    <div class="eq center">
      <span class="m"><i>α</i><sub>adjusted</sub> = <i>α</i> / <i>k</i> = 0.05 / 5 = 0.01</span>
    </div>
    <p>A row now counts as a meaningful imbalance only if its p-value is below 0.01. In Table 1 the
      smallest p-value is `r formatC(min(demo$p.value), format = "f", digits = 3)`, which is above 0.01, so
      the table as a whole gives no evidence that the groups differ. The star was a false alarm of the
      kind we should expect to see in about one row out of every twenty.</p>

    <p>The joint F-test in the last row of Table 1 reaches the same conclusion in a single step. Instead
      of five tests, it asks one question: do the five characteristics, taken together, predict which
      students were assigned to treatment? With p = `r formatC(demo.f.p, format = "f", digits = 3)`
      `r if (demo.f.p >= 0.05) "(above 0.05), they do not, so there is no evidence of imbalance." else "(below 0.05), they do, which would point to a real imbalance."`
      Because it is one test, it is compared with the ordinary <span class="m">α = 0.05</span>, with no
      correction needed.</p>

    <div class="callout">
      <span class="lbl">Where the correction applies</span>
      <p>Bonferroni is a rule for an <strong>omnibus test</strong>: many tests run together to answer one
        yes-or-no question, such as "are these groups equivalent at baseline?" It is not needed for
        the group contrasts in Section one, where each difference between study groups matters in its own
        right. A control group that started out low is a problem whatever the other contrasts show.</p>
    </div>

    <h3>Simulating 1,000 balance tables</h3>
    <p>How often does the unadjusted rule (any row with p &lt; .05) flag a perfectly randomized study,
      and how does that change as the table gets longer? We simulate 20 baseline attributes, added to the
      balance table in this order:</p>
```

```{r tbl-covlist, results="asis"}
cov.desc <- c(
  "Mother's education (years)", "Father's education (years)", "Family income ($1,000s)",
  "Black (0/1)", "Hispanic (0/1)", "Asian (0/1)", "Female (0/1)",
  "Free or reduced-price lunch (0/1)", "English learner (0/1)", "Special education (0/1)",
  "Prior math score", "Prior reading score", "Age (months)", "Days absent last year",
  "Household size", "Single-parent household (0/1)", "Changed schools last year (0/1)",
  "Books at home", "Homework hours per week", "Attended preschool (0/1)")
half <- 10
rows <- paste0("<tr><td class=\"l\">", 1:half, ". ", cov.desc[1:half], "</td><td class=\"l\">",
               (half + 1):20, ". ", cov.desc[(half + 1):20], "</td></tr>", collapse = "\n")
html('<div class="table-scroll"><table class="num-table">',
     '<caption>Baseline covariates</caption>',
     '<thead><tr><th>Covariates 1&ndash;10</th><th style="text-align:left">Covariates 11&ndash;20</th></tr></thead>',
     '<tbody>', rows, '</tbody></table></div>')
```

```{=html}
    <p>For each covariate we run a two-sample t-test of the difference in means between treatment and
      control. The standard rule is: if any test is significant at p &lt; .05, the groups are "not
      equivalent." We simulate 1,000 separate studies. Each one draws a fresh set of 200 students and
      a fresh lottery, so every difference is due to chance alone. A balance table with
      <span class="m"><i>k</i></span> rows uses the first <span class="m"><i>k</i></span> covariates.</p>

    <p>We also apply two corrected rules:</p>
    <ul>
      <li><strong>Bonferroni:</strong> a row counts as significant only if
        <span class="m">p &lt; 0.05 / <i>k</i></span>. With 10 covariates the threshold is 0.005.</li>
      <li><strong>Joint F-test:</strong> regress the treatment indicator on all
        <span class="m"><i>k</i></span> covariates and test whether they jointly predict assignment.
        One omnibus test, one p-value, compared with 0.05.</li>
    </ul>

    <figure class="fig">
```

```{r fig-covariates, fig.alt="The share of studies flagged as unbalanced rises from 5% with one covariate to over 60% with twenty under the unadjusted rule, while the Bonferroni and joint F-test rules stay near 5%."}
fig_covariates()
```

```{=html}
    </figure>
    <p class="figcap">Share of 1,000 perfectly randomized studies that the balance check would declare
      unbalanced, by number of covariates tested.</p>
```

```{r tbl-covariates, results="asis"}
show <- results
rows <- paste0("<tr", ifelse(show$k %in% c(1, 5, 10, 20), ' class="flag"', ""), "><td class=\"l\">",
               show$k, "</td><td class=\"hi\">", pct(show$any.sig, 1), "</td><td>",
               pct(show$expected, 1), "</td><td>", num(show$avg.sig, 2), "</td><td class=\"ok\">",
               pct(show$bonf, 1), "</td><td>", pct(show$joint.F, 1), "</td></tr>", collapse = "\n")
html('<div class="table-scroll"><table class="num-table">',
     '<caption>1,000 randomized studies per row, 100 treated and 100 controls</caption>',
     '<thead><tr><th>Covariates tested (<span class="m"><i>k</i></span>)</th>',
     '<th>Studies with any difference at p &lt; .05</th>',
     '<th>Theory: <span class="m">1 &minus; 0.95<sup><i>k</i></sup></span></th>',
     '<th>Average number of significant differences</th>',
     '<th>Studies with any difference, Bonferroni (p &lt; .05 / <span class="m"><i>k</i></span>)</th>',
     '<th>Studies failing joint F-test (p &lt; .05)</th></tr></thead>',
     '<tbody>', rows, '</tbody></table></div>')
```

```{=html}
    <h3>Reading the table</h3>
    <ul>
      <li><strong>The unadjusted rule fails more and more valid studies.</strong> With one covariate, a
        study is flagged `r pct(results$any.sig[1])` of the time, close to the nominal 5% (the gap is simulation noise). With 10 covariates,
        `r pct(results$any.sig[10])` of perfectly randomized studies show at least one "significant"
        imbalance; with 20, `r pct(results$any.sig[20])` do. Here the tests are nearly independent
        (the covariates are simulated independently), so the rate tracks the formula
        <span class="m">1 &minus; 0.95<sup><i>k</i></sup></span>.</li>
      <li><strong>The average count rises in a straight line:</strong> about
        <span class="m">0.05 &times; <i>k</i></span>, or one false alarm for every 20 covariates.
        Finding one significant row in a 20-row balance table is exactly what a successful
        randomization looks like.</li>
      <li><strong>Both corrected rules hold the error rate near 5%</strong> no matter how many
        covariates are tested. They answer the question we actually care about: <em>is there evidence
        that the groups differ, taking the whole table into account?</em></li>
    </ul>

    <div class="callout">
      <span class="lbl">Bonferroni or joint F-test?</span>
      <p>Bonferroni is simple and is the rule used in the lab: compare each p-value with
        <span class="m">α / <i>k</i></span>. It is conservative when covariates are correlated (parents'
        education and family income usually are), because it treats overlapping tests as separate
        chances to err. The joint F-test accounts for correlation automatically and gives one answer for
        the whole table. Either is defensible. Testing each row at 0.05 is not.</p>
    </div>

    <details class="code">
      <summary>R code for this section</summary>

```{=html}
    </details>
  </section>

  <!-- ================================================================== -->
  <section id="takeaways">
    <div class="sec-head">
      <p class="num">Section three</p>
      <h2>Takeaways</h2>
      <p class="sub">How to check whether a randomization was happy.</p>
    </div>

    <ol class="checklist">
      <li><strong>Always check balance, even after random assignment.</strong> Randomization makes the
        groups equal on average across all possible lotteries, not in the one lottery your study got.</li>
      <li><strong>Count your tests before you read them.</strong> Five groups means 10 contrasts; 20
        covariates means 20 tests. At <span class="m">α = .05</span>, expect about one false alarm per 20
        tests.</li>
      <li><strong>Adjust the decision rule for the whole table.</strong> Use
        <span class="m">α / <i>k</i></span> (Bonferroni) or a single joint F-test. The unadjusted rule
        rejects most valid randomizations once the table has more than about 14 rows.</li>
      <li><strong>Look at the size of differences, not just their significance.</strong> In a large
        study a trivial difference can be significant; in a small study a substantively large difference
        can fail to reach significance. Report standardized differences (difference in means divided by
        the standard deviation) alongside p-values.</li>
      <li><strong>Small studies should not rely on luck.</strong> With few units per group, use
        stratified or blocked randomization (like the tranches in the reading) to guarantee balance on
        the variables that matter most.</li>
      <li><strong>Include baseline covariates as controls.</strong> Adjusting for them in the outcome
        regression corrects for whatever chance imbalance remains and makes the impact estimate more
        precise.</li>
    </ol>
  </section>
